question: An estates officer asked for a maintenance summary covering all eight regional depots, plus a cost estimate and a recommended priority order for each. The reply is polished and reads convincingly. What should she do first?
options: A) Read the summary closely for anything that sounds implausible, since a fluent draft rarely omits requested material.
B) Forward the summary to the depot managers so that each of them can tell her whether their own section is missing.
C) Ask Claude to confirm that its summary addressed every part of the request, and rely on the answer it gives.
D) Lay her original request beside the reply and mark which of the depots and required elements are actually covered.
correct_answers: D) Lay her original request beside the reply and mark which of the depots and required elements are actually covered.
explanations: Plausibility screening catches odd-sounding claims but is blind to omission: a section that was never written cannot sound wrong. Fluency is not evidence of coverage, so this misses the most likely defect in a multi-part request.

Distributing the draft pushes a basic completeness check onto colleagues and risks an incomplete document circulating as if it were finished. It is also slower than simply comparing the reply with the request she wrote.

Claude is not a reliable auditor of its own coverage, and treating its self-assessment as confirmation makes it a singular source of truth on the very point in doubt. The request itself is the standard to compare against.

Correct. Completeness is judged against the original request, not against how good the answer sounds. Checking the reply element by element against what she asked for immediately exposes any depot or required component that was dropped.
